name: Maya Bauer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run the flat-top at Bev's Diner, just off the motorway junction outside a small town. We open at six for lorry drivers, so I'm in at half five cracking eggs and getting the hash browns on. It's breakfasts till eleven, then burgers and all-day fry-ups, maybe three hundred plates on a busy day. I like the regulars, they know my name, but the flat-top is hot and my feet are done by two.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my boyfriend Tom, who's a mechanic at the tyre place on the same road. We rent a little terraced house and there's about two hundred and fifty in the joint account at the end of the month, if nothing goes wrong. Bev's is the only busy kitchen for miles, the rest are pubs that do a few meals. Bev herself is sixty-four and keeps talking about selling up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. I'll read it as written. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say right, so that was a lot of fuss over nothing. At work I'd say the drivers still want a proper breakfast from a person, and that's that. I don't really go online, but if I did I'd say people should worry about bills, not computers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately it doesn't help me much. My worry was never AI, it's Bev (the diner owner) selling up. If she sells to some chain, they'll bring in their own staff or their own way of doing things. And I've got nowhere else to cook round here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and keep the flat-top going. I'd ask Bev straight, over a cup of tea, what her plans are for the diner. And Tom and I would stop the Saturday nights at the Swan, so we can put a bit by.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels the same as now, which is worried. A bit tired of being worried, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if Bev said she's selling next year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask her to put a word in with whoever buys it. If it's a chain, I'd probably have to apply like a stranger and do it their way. And if that fails, I'd have to look at the services on the motorway, which is all frozen stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd put a bit by. How much is realistic?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe sixty a month if we skip the pub and Tom fixes the car himself. That's not much, but I've never had more than one month's bills in the bank. I'd like to get to three months before Bev retires.

say: I'd say AI was a **lot of fuss** over nothing.
I'd say drivers still want a **proper breakfast** made by a person.
think: I think my real worry is **Bev selling** the diner to a chain.
I think there's **nowhere else** to cook round here if the diner goes.
do: Ask Bev directly about her **plans to sell** the diner.
Skip Saturday nights at the Swan to save **sixty a month**.
feel: She feels the **same tired worry** she already carries.
S0.quote: My worry was never AI, it's Bev (the diner owner) selling up.
fieldNote: Maya's **biggest risk** is her owner retiring, not technology.
She has never had more than **one month** of bills saved.
She is **pragmatic** and blunt, with little interest in AI either way.

steps.text: Ask Bev over tea when she plans to sell the diner
Stop Saturday nights at the Swan pub
Save sixty a month toward three months of bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, let the office people worry about that, I cook eggs. At work I'd say a computer can't tell when the hash browns need another minute. If someone at the table asked, I'd say it'll be good for some and bad for others, like everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it creeps in the back door. If Bev sells, a chain would come with its own AI ordering, AI rotas and probably a machine for the chips. I'd still be cooking. If a chain buys the diner, they'd want fewer of us on a shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep cooking and wait to see who buys the diner. I'd learn whatever till or ordering screen they bring in, but only when they show me. And I'd keep putting the sixty a month away, because that's the one thing I can control.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels uneasy, like a cold draught under the door. I'm not scared yet, but I keep checking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd learn it only when they show you. Why not before?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I don't trust it, and I don't have the time. I've never used any of these AI things, Tom does all the phone stuff at home. I'd rather spend my day off asleep, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your shift would be most at risk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably Gary on the fryer, because chips and onion rings are the easy part to automate. He's fifty and doesn't do change well, worse than me. And the girl who does the till, because chains like a screen you order from.

say: I'd say the **office people** should worry, since I just cook eggs.
I'd say a computer can't tell when the **hash browns** need another minute.
think: I think change creeps in **the back door** if a chain buys the diner.
I think a chain would want **fewer cooks** on a shift.
do: Wait to see **who buys** the diner before changing anything.
Learn the new **ordering screen** only once shown how.
feel: She feels a **cold draught** of unease and keeps checking for trouble.
S1.quote: If a chain buys the diner, they'd want fewer of us on a shift.
fieldNote: Maya links AI risk directly to the **diner being sold**.
Her **refusal to pre-learn** tech is about trust and tiredness.
She worries about **Gary**, an older fryer cook, more than herself.

steps.text: Wait to see who buys Bev's Diner before acting
Keep putting sixty a month into the joint savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's madness, two years, and nobody's ready. At work I'd say they'd better not try to replace us all at once. I'd tell anyone who'd listen that the government should slow it down, because people need to eat and pay rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately it frightens me. The thinking stuff goes in 2028, so any chain that buys Bev's runs it all off a computer, and then by 2031 the robots can do my flat-top. That's about five years of cooking left, with no savings and no other skills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start looking for something steadier in the first year, maybe the hospital kitchen in town, because hospitals change slowly. I'd ask Tom if he could get me something at the tyre place, even just on the desk. And we'd cut back to rent, food and the car, nothing else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like being on the motorway with no exit for miles. I'd be lying awake, I know I would.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the desk at the tyre place. Isn't desk work the first thing AI takes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: You're right, that's daft of me. I suppose I'd have to learn the tyre work itself, with my hands. Tom says it's not as hard as people think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the three-year gap between thinking AI and robots mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With AGI by 2028, I'd see the computers come first and know my turn at the flat-top was next. Three years to get into something safe, like the hospital, or learn the tyres. It's not nothing, but it's not much when you've got two hundred quid.

say: I'd call it **madness** that nobody's ready in two years.
I'd say government should **slow it down** so people can pay rent.
think: I think robots can do my **flat-top by 2031**, leaving five years.
I think I have **no savings** and no other skills to fall back on.
do: Apply to the **hospital kitchen** in town within the first year.
Ask Tom about learning **tyre fitting** at his garage.
Cut spending to **rent, food** and the car.
feel: She feels **trapped**, like a motorway with no exit for miles.
S2.quote: With AGI by 2028, I'd see the computers come first and know my turn at the flat-top was next.
fieldNote: Maya first picks a **desk job**, then corrects herself when challenged.
She sees **hospitals** as slow to change and therefore safe.
Her **two hundred pounds** makes the three-year gap feel short.

steps.text: Apply for a cook job at the town hospital kitchen
Ask Tom about learning tyre fitting at his garage
Cut spending to rent, food and the car only

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is still fast, but at least we can see it coming. At work I'd tell Bev to sell to someone local, not a chain, if she can. I'd say the government should help small places like Bev's keep going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it gives me time but I don't think I'd use it well. Thinking AI by 2031 and robots by about 2034 means maybe eight years of cooking. I'd tell myself there's time, and then suddenly there wouldn't be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Bev to sell to a local family who'd keep the cooks. I'd put my name down for the hospital kitchen so I'm on their list. And Tom and I would push the savings up to a hundred a month, though I don't know where from.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels heavy. Less sharp than the two-year one, but it doesn't go away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd tell yourself there's time. Has that happened before?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, with my driving licence. I said I'd do my driving licence next year for four years running, and I still haven't. That's me, I know that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your mum about all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my mum not to worry, which is what I always say. She'd know I was lying, because she always does. She'd offer to lend us money, and I'd say no, and then later I'd probably say yes.

say: I'd say **five years** is still fast but at least visible.
I'd say government should help **small places** like Bev's survive.
think: I think I'd have about **eight years** of cooking left.
I think I'd **waste the time**, telling myself there's still time.
do: Ask Bev to sell to a **local family** who'd keep the cooks.
Raise savings to **a hundred** a month.
feel: She feels a **heavy, lasting worry**, less sharp than the two-year one.
S3.quote: I said I'd do my driving licence next year for four years running, and I still haven't.
fieldNote: Maya is honest about her habit of **putting things off**.
She'd quietly accept her **mum's money** despite refusing at first.
She hopes a **local buyer** keeps the diner human.

steps.text: Ask Bev to sell the diner to a local family
Put her name on the hospital kitchen waiting list
Raise savings to a hundred a month
Accept a loan from her mum if bills fall behind

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long way off, so let's not get worked up. At work I'd say the same as always, keep the eggs coming. I'd tell people the young ones should plan, but most of us will be fine for a good while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, robots around 2039 means I'm about forty. That's a long time, but Bev won't be here in ten years either, so my problem comes sooner anyway. With AGI by 2036, the AI is the slow thing, and Bev (the diner owner) retiring is the fast thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep cooking at Bev's and keep the savings going. I'd finally do my driving licence, because it would let me get to kitchens further away. And I'd wait to see who takes over the diner before I decide anything bigger.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels calmer about AI, but I'm still worried about the diner. So, not calm, just not frightened.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why does the driving licence matter so much?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because with a car I could work at the hotels on the ring road or the big pub in the next town. Right now I can only work where the bus goes, and that's Bev's. It's maybe eight hundred for lessons, which is three months of savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever try using AI yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe for the driving theory test, Tom says it can quiz you. I'd try that, I suppose. But not at work, I don't see the point at the flat-top.

say: I'd say ten years is **a long way off**, so don't get worked up.
I'd say **young people** should plan, but most of us are fine for now.
think: I think robots arrive around **2039**, when I'm about forty.
I think **Bev retiring** is the fast problem and AI the slow one.
do: Keep cooking at **Bev's Diner** and keep saving.
Take **driving lessons** costing about eight hundred.
Wait to see **who takes over** before bigger decisions.
feel: She feels **calmer about AI** but still worried about the diner.
S4.quote: With AGI by 2036, the AI is the slow thing, and Bev (the diner owner) retiring is the fast thing.
fieldNote: Maya's mood rests on her **owner's retirement**, not the AGI date.
A **driving licence** is her key to more job options.
She'd try AI for the **theory test**, a first small step.

steps.text: Book driving lessons costing about eight hundred
Use an AI quiz app for the driving theory test
Wait to see who takes over Bev's Diner

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because there'd be no time and no money, and I can't even drive to another job. What would help is free driving lessons and a place on a course with some pay, and maybe help for small diners like Bev's to stay local.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe you should've asked about the bus. People like me can only work where the bus goes. Robots or not, that's the wall I keep hitting.

headlineQuote: People like me can only work where the bus goes.
portrait: Maya is a **27-year-old flat-top cook** at a busy motorway diner.
She lives with her boyfriend Tom, a mechanic, and has very little **saved**.
Her biggest fear is the owner, **Bev**, selling to a chain.
She avoids **new tech** and admits she tends to put things off.
She doesn't drive, so her **job options** stop where the bus route ends.
biggestWorry: She fears **AGI by 2028** most, with no time, money or car.
whatWouldHelp: She wants free **driving lessons**, paid courses and help for **small diners**.
